case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a district court’s denial (at summary judgment) of a federal contractor’s “derivative sovereign immunity” defense under Yearsley is immediately appealable under the collateral-order doctrine rather than only after final judgment.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1291 (final-judgment rule) and the judicially created collateral-order doctrine (from Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp.).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: GEO Group argues that Yearsley “derivative sovereign immunity” functions like an immunity from suit (not merely a defense to liability) when a contractor performs work authorized and directed by the federal government. Because the asserted protection would be lost if the contractor must endure discovery and trial, GEO contends an erroneous denial is effectively unreviewable after final judgment and thus qualifies for immediate appeal as a collateral order. GEO and supporting amici further emphasize strong public interests: contractors perform essential government functions, and exposing them to burdensome litigation (before appellate correction) will deter contracting, raise costs, and disrupt government programs—especially where the United States itself retains sovereign immunity and plaintiffs target contractors as the only available deep pocket.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that Yearsley is not a true immunity from suit but a limited merits-linked defense: it turns on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authorization and conformed to that authorization—issues often entangled with factual disputes. They contend collateral-order review would improperly expand a narrow doctrine and invite piecemeal appeals in ordinary summary-judgment denials, contrary to § 1291’s final-judgment rule. Respondents also maintain that existing mechanisms (final-judgment appeal, discretionary interlocutory review under § 1292(b), mandamus in extraordinary cases) are adequate, and that policy arguments about contractor protection and litigation burdens are for Congress, not a judicial expansion of collateral-order jurisdiction.
key_precedents: Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. (1940)
Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. (1949)
CACI Premier Technology, Inc. v. Al Shimari (141 S. Ct. 2850 (2021) (statement respecting denial / SG invitation in related collateral-order context))

John Roberts.reasoning: I remain with the Respondent because the petitioner’s best point—pressed most forcefully by analogy to Mitchell—that Yearsley supplies an immunity-like “right not to stand trial” does not satisfy Cohen as we have insisted in Digital Equipment and Will v. Hallock. As Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, Yearsley denials at summary judgment typically depend on fact-bound, merits-adjacent questions about the scope of federal authorization and conformity, placing them on the Johnson v. Jones side of the line and defeating Cohen’s “complete separateness” requirement. Even accepting the litigation-burden concern, post-judgment review ordinarily remedies any error, and §1292(b) certification or (in truly extraordinary cases) mandamus supplies the targeted safety valve without creating a broad new collateral-order category. Under a minimalist approach protective of §1291’s final-judgment rule and institutional legitimacy, we should decide narrowly: no categorical collateral-order jurisdiction for Yearsley denials at summary judgment, particularly where factual disputes drive the denial.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest argument—that a Yearsley denial is like qualified immunity and therefore immediately appealable under Mitchell—does not overcome § 1291’s textual limitation to “final decisions,” and we should not enlarge Cohen’s narrow, judge-made exception absent a tight fit. As Justice Barrett stresses via Johnson v. Jones, Yearsley denials at summary judgment typically rest on disputed facts about authorization and conformity, so interlocutory review would devolve into impermissible evidence-sufficiency appeals rather than a clean legal question. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Digital Equipment and Will v. Hallock reinforces that post-judgment review generally suffices and that “effective unreviewability” is not satisfied merely by the burdens of trial. If Congress believes federal contractors need broader interlocutory review, it can authorize it; it is not our role to rewrite § 1291 through an expanded collateral-order doctrine.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the Mitchell-style claim that Yearsley is an entitlement not to stand trial, but that analogy breaks down because the Yearsley inquiry (valid federal authorization and conformity to it) is typically fact- and merits-entangled, putting it on the Johnson v. Jones side rather than presenting a clean legal question. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Will v. Hallock and Digital Equipment reinforces that we should not expand Cohen’s “small class” where post-judgment review is available and interlocutory appeals would predictably proliferate. Justice Barrett’s emphasis that fact-dispute summary-judgment denials would devolve into impermissible evidence-sufficiency appeals underscores the administrability problem with recognizing a new collateral-order category. Even if a rare case poses a purely legal Yearsley issue, § 1292(b) certification or mandamus provides a narrow safety valve without rewriting § 1291 through judge-made enlargement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains the Mitchell analogy—that Yearsley confers an immunity-like right not to stand trial—but, as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett stress, Yearsley denials at summary judgment typically hinge on disputed facts about authorization and conformity, putting them on the Johnson v. Jones side of the line as impermissible evidence-sufficiency interlocutory appeals. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about Digital Equipment and Will v. Hallock reinforces that we should not enlarge Cohen’s “small class” to cover a routine, merits-entangled defense where post-judgment review can correct error. Even accepting Justice Thomas’s textual emphasis on § 1291, the pragmatic concern is the same: a new appeal-as-of-right category would systematically delay merits adjudication and burden injured plaintiffs, while § 1292(b) and mandamus remain adequate safety valves for the genuinely exceptional, purely legal case.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point is the Mitchell-style claim that Yearsley is an immunity from suit and therefore “effectively unreviewable” after trial, but Justice Barrett is right that Johnson v. Jones draws a firm line against interlocutory review of summary-judgment denials that hinge on fact disputes. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, Cohen requires an issue “completely separate from the merits,” and Yearsley’s authorization-and-conformity inquiries are typically merits-adjacent and record-bound, so immediate appeal would devolve into forbidden evidence-sufficiency policing. Even if a subset of cases presents a clean legal Yearsley question, Will v. Hallock and Digital Equipment counsel against creating new categorical collateral-order classes when § 1292(b) and (rarely) mandamus can handle the exceptional case without distorting § 1291’s finality principle. Post-judgment review remains an adequate corrective, so the Cohen requirements are not met.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the Mitchell analogy—that Yearsley is an entitlement not to stand trial—but Chief Justice Roberts correctly invokes Digital Equipment and Will v. Hallock to warn against enlarging Cohen beyond its narrow, categorical classes. As Justice Barrett emphasizes, Yearsley denials at summary judgment typically hinge on disputed facts about authorization and conformity, making them merits-entangled and resembling the evidence-sufficiency appeals Johnson v. Jones bars. Even where a case presents a relatively clean legal question, that does not justify creating a new collateral-order category; § 1292(b) certification and (rare) mandamus can address exceptional circumstances without rewriting § 1291’s final-decision rule. On a textualist, separation-of-powers view, any broader interlocutory appeal right for contractors is for Congress to provide, not this Court to invent.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the Mitchell analogy—that Yearsley is an immunity-like entitlement not to stand trial and thus should be immediately appealable—but that framing runs into Cohen’s separateness requirement because Yearsley usually asks whether the contractor acted within valid federal authorization and conformed to it, which is merits-adjacent and often fact-bound in the Johnson v. Jones sense. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on Will v. Hallock and Digital Equipment reinforces that we should not create a new collateral-order category where post-judgment review remains available and interlocutory review would predictably generate piecemeal appeals. Justice Barrett’s point is also persuasive that attempting to carve out only “purely legal” Yearsley denials would be an unadministrable, case-by-case expansion of a doctrine that must remain categorical; § 1292(b) certification and (in truly extraordinary cases) mandamus are the appropriate safety valves. Under an institutionalist and precedent-respecting approach, nothing here justifies enlarging this judge-made exception to § 1291.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the Mitchell analogy—that Yearsley is an immunity-like entitlement not to stand trial—but that framing does not fit Cohen’s “small class” as administered in Digital Equipment and Will v. Hallock because Yearsley’s authorization-and-conformity questions are commonly merits-adjacent and fact-bound. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, once the denial rests on genuine disputes of material fact, interlocutory review would force appellate courts into the evidence-sufficiency policing Johnson v. Jones forbids, rather than deciding a clean legal issue as in Mitchell. Chief Justice Roberts’s institutional point reinforces my textualist reluctance to expand a judge-made exception to § 1291 where post-judgment review remains available and § 1292(b) (and in extraordinary cases, mandamus) can handle the rare purely legal Yearsley dispute. Nothing in colleagues’ discussion undermines that the separateness and effective-unreviewability prongs are not met categorically here, so the order is not immediately appealable.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the Mitchell-style claim that Yearsley is an immunity from suit whose value is lost if a contractor must endure discovery and trial, but that contention cannot satisfy Cohen’s requirements in the run of cases. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, the Yearsley authorization-and-conformity inquiry is commonly intertwined with the merits and often turns on disputed facts, making it look like Johnson v. Jones–type evidence-sufficiency review rather than a clean, purely legal entitlement. And even accepting some litigation-burden costs, Will v. Hallock and Digital Equipment (as Roberts notes) counsel against expanding a judge-made, “narrow class” exception to § 1291 where post-judgment review remains available and Congress has provided targeted safety valves like § 1292(b) (and, in extraordinary cases, mandamus). On administrability and procedural fairness grounds, creating a routine interlocutory-appeal category for contractors would invite piecemeal litigation and systematically delay plaintiffs’ day in court without a sufficiently separate, effectively unreviewable right at stake.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies the final-judgment rule, and the collateral-order doctrine remains a “narrow” and “stringent” exception that we have repeatedly refused to expand. Under Cohen and Will v. Hallock, a denial of Yearsley protection at summary judgment generally fails at least the second and third prongs: whether the contractor acted within valid federal authorization and conformed to it is typically intertwined with the merits and fact disputes, and any error can be remedied on appeal after final judgment rather than being “effectively unreviewable.” Unlike qualified or Eleventh Amendment immunity recognized for immediate appeal in Mitchell, Yearsley is better understood as a merits-linked defense to liability, and existing avenues like § 1292(b) certification or mandamus in extraordinary cases provide adequate safety valves without inviting piecemeal appeals. Preserving institutional legitimacy and the settled limits on collateral-order jurisdiction counsels against creating a new immediately appealable category here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1291’s text limits appellate jurisdiction to “final decisions,” and the collateral-order doctrine is a narrow, judicially created exception that should not be expanded absent a clear fit within Cohen’s strict criteria. A Yearsley defense, as articulated in Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. (1940), turns on whether the contractor acted pursuant to valid federal authorization and conformed to that authorization—questions frequently intertwined with the merits and factual disputes, failing Cohen’s “completely separate from the merits” requirement. Unlike qualified immunity in Mitchell v. Forsyth (1985), which can present a pure legal “right not to stand trial,” Yearsley commonly resembles the fact-bound determinations that Johnson v. Jones (1995) held are not immediately appealable. Any policy-based expansion of interlocutory appeals for federal contractors is properly for Congress to enact, not for courts to graft onto § 1291.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies a strong final-judgment rule, and Cohen’s collateral-order exception remains a “small class” that we have repeatedly refused to expand. A Yearsley defense turns on whether the contractor acted pursuant to valid federal authorization and within the scope of that authorization—questions frequently entangled with disputed facts and the merits, making these orders unlike the purely legal qualified-immunity question in Mitchell v. Forsyth and instead akin to the fact-bound category we held not immediately appealable in Johnson v. Jones. Because erroneous denial of Yearsley can be reviewed after final judgment (and, in appropriate cases, via § 1292(b) certification or mandamus), it is not “effectively unreviewable” in the sense required by the collateral-order doctrine. Treating routine summary-judgment denials of Yearsley as immediately appealable would invite piecemeal appeals and undermine § 1291’s practical operation, a policy choice better left to Congress.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies a strong final-judgment rule, and the collateral-order doctrine under Cohen is a “narrow” exception that should not be expanded to routine summary-judgment denials. A Yearsley defense is merits-linked because it turns on whether the contractor acted pursuant to valid federal authorization and conformed to it, an inquiry that commonly depends on disputed facts and thus resembles the “evidence sufficiency” determinations Johnson v. Jones held are not immediately appealable. Unlike qualified immunity in Mitchell v. Forsyth—which turns on a separable, predominantly legal question (clearly established law)—Yearsley does not categorically provide an entitlement to avoid trial that is “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment. Adequate alternatives (post-judgment review, discretionary § 1292(b) certification, and mandamus in extraordinary cases) protect government interests without inviting piecemeal appeals that would delay relief for vulnerable plaintiffs.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies a strong final-judgment rule, and Cohen’s collateral-order exception remains “narrow and selective,” requiring (among other things) that the issue be effectively unreviewable after final judgment and completely separate from the merits. A Yearsley defense turns on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authorization and complied with government directions—questions that are commonly fact-entangled and overlap with the plaintiff’s theory of wrongdoing, making this category of orders fail Cohen’s “separate from the merits” requirement and resemble the nonappealable fact-sufficiency disputes barred by Johnson v. Jones. Unlike qualified immunity in Mitchell v. Forsyth, which permits immediate appeal only for the purely legal “clearly established law” question, Yearsley denials at summary judgment will often require sorting disputed facts about authorization and compliance, and any error can be corrected on appeal after final judgment. If additional interlocutory review is warranted for contractors, Congress can provide it expressly, and existing safety valves (§ 1292(b) certification and mandamus) address exceptional cases without expanding collateral-order jurisdiction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies Congress’s final-judgment rule, and this Court has repeatedly insisted the collateral-order doctrine remain a “narrow class” with “stringent” conditions. Digital Equipment and Will v. Hallock teach that interlocutory appeal is reserved for orders denying a true entitlement not to stand trial, not for defenses closely intertwined with the merits; Yearsley turns on whether the contractor acted pursuant to valid federal authorization and conformed to it, inquiries often bound up with disputed facts and thus not “completely separate” in the Cohen sense (cf. Johnson v. Jones). Any asserted policy need for broader interlocutory review is for Congress to supply through § 1292 or otherwise, not for courts to expand a judge-made exception to § 1291.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1291 and this Court’s narrow collateral-order doctrine, immediate appeal is reserved for a small class of orders that conclusively resolve an important issue completely separate from the merits and that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment. Yearsley’s so-called “derivative sovereign immunity” is typically a fact-bound, merits-linked defense turning on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authorization and conformed to it, so denials at summary judgment often rest on disputed evidence and are not “completely separate” in the way Mitchell v. Forsyth permitted for purely legal qualified-immunity questions. Johnson v. Jones reinforces that we do not allow collateral-order appeals where the denial turns on “evidence sufficiency” and factual disputes, because that would invite piecemeal review inconsistent with § 1291’s final-judgment rule. Any policy-based expansion for government contractors can be addressed through existing avenues (final-judgment review, § 1292(b), or mandamus in extraordinary cases) or by Congress rather than by broadening collateral-order jurisdiction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies the final-judgment rule, and the collateral-order doctrine is a narrow, judicially created exception that applies only when an order conclusively resolves an important issue that is completely separate from the merits and effectively unreviewable after final judgment. A Yearsley defense turns on whether the contractor acted pursuant to valid federal authorization and conformed to that authorization—questions that frequently overlap with merits and, at summary judgment, may depend on contested facts—so it does not fit Cohen’s “completely separate” requirement. Mitchell v. Forsyth allowed immediate appeal because qualified immunity presents a primarily legal “clearly established law” question, but Johnson v. Jones holds that when the denial rests on the existence of genuine factual disputes, collateral-order review is unavailable; Yearsley denials at summary judgment commonly resemble the latter. Given that alternative avenues (final-judgment review and discretionary § 1292(b) interlocutory certification) exist, expanding collateral-order jurisdiction here would be inconsistent with § 1291’s text and this Court’s insistence on methodological restraint in interlocutory appeals.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1291’s final-judgment rule permits immediate appeal only for the “small class” of collateral orders under Cohen, and a Yearsley ruling typically fails Cohen’s “separate from the merits” and “effectively unreviewable” prongs because it turns on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authorization and conformed to it—fact-bound issues intertwined with liability. Mitchell allows collateral-order review for qualified-immunity denials only insofar as they present a “purely legal” question (e.g., clearly established law), while Johnson bars interlocutory appeals from summary-judgment denials that hinge on whether the record shows a genuine dispute of material fact; Yearsley determinations at summary judgment commonly resemble the latter. Practical concerns about litigation burdens and deterrence of contracting do not justify expanding a judge-made jurisdictional exception where Congress has provided alternative mechanisms (e.g., § 1292(b)) and where piecemeal appeals would undermine efficiency and procedural fairness in ordinary civil litigation. Accordingly, denials of Yearsley “derivative sovereign immunity” at summary judgment should be reviewed after final judgment absent statutory authorization for interlocutory appeal.

case_analysis.petitioner_position: GEO Group argues that Yearsley “derivative sovereign immunity” functions like an immunity from suit (not merely a defense to liability) when a contractor acts pursuant to valid federal authorization, so the core benefit is avoiding the burdens of litigation itself. Because that protection is effectively lost if the contractor must proceed through discovery and trial before appealing, GEO contends that an interlocutory appeal should be available as a collateral order—similar in structure to qualified-immunity appeals—especially given the government’s strong interest in ensuring contractors will perform sensitive governmental functions without being forced into protracted litigation whenever plaintiffs allege wrongdoing.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that Yearsley is not the sort of immunity that confers a right to avoid litigation; at most it is a merits defense (or a limited jurisdictional/attribution rule) that depends on fact-intensive questions about authorization and compliance with government directions. Because denials of Yearsley commonly turn on disputed facts and are intertwined with the merits, they do not satisfy the collateral-order requirements (including being “completely separate from the merits”). Respondents emphasize that expanding collateral-order appeals would undermine the final-judgment rule, and that any new interlocutory appeal right for contractors should come from Congress (e.g., through § 1292 or a statutory amendment), not judicial expansion of Cohen.

I therefore would affirm on narrow grounds: Yearsley denials at summary judgment are not categorically immediately appealable under Cohen because they are not completely separate from the merits and are generally reviewable after final judgment.

A Yearsley denial at summary judgment typically turns on fact-bound questions about the scope of federal authorization and the contractor’s compliance with government directions, so the issue is not “completely separate from the merits” and is often an “evidence sufficiency” dispute of the sort Johnson v. Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1291’s text grants appellate jurisdiction over “final decisions,” and the collateral-order doctrine of Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp., 337 U.S. 541 (1949), is a narrow, judge-made gloss that must not be expanded beyond its limited historical function. Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1291 limits our review to "final decisions," and Cohen’s collateral-order doctrine remains a "small class" of exceptions that this Court has repeatedly described as "stringent" and "narrow." Digital Equipment Corp. v. Desktop Direct, Inc., 511 U.S. 863, 868 (1994); Mohawk Indus., Inc. v. Carpenter, 558 U.S. 100, 106-07 (2009). A Yearsley defense typically turns on fact-bound questions about the scope of federal authorization and compliance with government directions, making denials at summary judgment neither "completely separate from the merits" nor reliably resolvable as a pure legal question in the way Mitchell v. Forsyth permits for qualified immunity; Johnson v. Jones further cautions against collateral appeals where the order rests on the sufficiency of factual disputes. 28 U.S.C. § 1291; Mitchell v. Forsyth, 472 U.S. 511 (1985); Johnson v. Jones, 515 U.S. 304 (1995). Whatever policy arguments favor interlocutory review for contractors, creating that additional appellate pathway is a matter for Congress (e.g., § 1292), not an expansion of Cohen by judicial decision.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1291’s final-judgment rule and this Court’s narrow collateral-order doctrine require that the issue be effectively unreviewable after final judgment and “completely separate from the merits.” Cohen v. Beneficial Indus. Loan Corp. (1949). Unlike qualified immunity in Mitchell v. Forsyth (1985), where interlocutory review is justified because the appeal turns on a pure question of law (“clearly established” law), Yearsley determinations commonly hinge on disputed, fact-intensive questions about the scope of federal authorization and compliance with governmental directions. Under Johnson v. Jones (1995), denials of asserted immunities at summary judgment are not immediately appealable when they rest on “evidence sufficiency” or disputed facts, and expanding Cohen here would undermine the workability of § 1291 absent congressional action (e.g., through § 1292).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1291 authorizes appeals from “final decisions,” and the collateral-order doctrine is a “narrow” and “stringent” exception that this Court has repeatedly refused to expand. Under Cohen and Van Cauwenberghe, a Yearsley denial typically fails at least the “completely separate from the merits” prong because it turns on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authorization and complied with government directions—questions often intertwined with the merits and fact-bound in the way Johnson v. Jones held not immediately appealable. It also falters on “effectively unreviewable” under Digital Equipment and Will v. Hallock, because Yearsley functions in many cases like a merits defense to liability rather than a category of immunity conferring a right “not to stand trial altogether.” Given Congress’s ability to provide interlocutory review via § 1292 or amendment, methodological consistency with our precedents counsels against enlarging Cohen here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1291’s final-judgment rule, as limited by Cohen, permits collateral-order appeals only for a narrow class of orders that are effectively unreviewable after final judgment and are completely separate from the merits. A Yearsley defense typically turns on fact-bound questions about the scope of federal authorization and whether the contractor complied with government directions, so denials at summary judgment often reflect “evidence sufficiency” determinations that Johnson v. Jones held are not immediately appealable, unlike the pure legal “clearly established law” issue in Mitchell v. Forsyth. Treating Yearsley as an immunity-from-suit for interlocutory review would expand Cohen in a way this Court has repeatedly cautioned against and would invite litigation-delaying appeals in precisely the merits-entwined category Digital Equipment warns must be assessed at the categorical level. Any broader interlocutory appeal right for contractors is better left to Congress under § 1292 or statutory amendment rather than judicial enlargement of § 1291.
